questions.prompt: What is the main goal of root cause analysis for a defect?
options: To find why the defect was introduced and why it escaped, so the process can be improved
To find who to blame
To fix the code faster
To close the defect report
questions.explanation: RCA targets causes in the process so similar defects are prevented. It is not about blame, and fixing or closing the defect is separate work.

questions.prompt: In a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram, what goes at the head of the fish?
options: The problem or effect being analysed
The person responsible
The final fix
The project budget
questions.explanation: The head holds the effect; the bones hold categories of possible causes, such as people, process, tools and environment.

questions.prompt: The 5 Whys technique always requires exactly five questions.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Five is a rule of thumb. You stop when you reach a cause the team can act on, which may take fewer or more steps.

questions.prompt: Which are good characteristics of a root cause statement? Select all that apply.
options: It points to something the team can change
It explains both introduction and escape where relevant
It is supported by evidence
It names an individual as the cause
questions.explanation: Actionable, complete and evidence-based causes lead to useful improvements. Naming individuals creates blame and discourages honest analysis.

questions.prompt: 5 Whys on a production timeout ends with "Because the developer made a mistake". What should the facilitator do?
options: Keep asking why the mistake was possible and why it was not caught, e.g. missing review or unclear requirement
Accept it and end the session
Discipline the developer
Skip RCA in future
questions.explanation: Human error is a starting point, not a root cause. Asking why the process allowed and missed it leads to systemic fixes.

questions.prompt: Why should teams analyse both why a defect was introduced and why it escaped testing?
options: Because prevention and detection gaps need different improvements
Because escape analysis is the only thing that matters
Because introduction analysis is the only thing that matters
Because it doubles the report length
questions.explanation: Introduction causes lead to prevention measures (requirements, design, coding); escape causes lead to detection measures (tests, reviews, monitoring). Both matter.

questions.prompt: When is a full root cause analysis most worth the effort?
options: For high-impact or recurring defects, where preventing recurrence pays back
For every cosmetic typo
Never, because defects are random
Only when a manager is angry
questions.explanation: RCA costs time, so it is best spent on severe, escaped or repeating issues. Defects have causes, and emotion is not a selection criterion.

questions.prompt: Three separate escaped defects this quarter involved time zones. Each RCA concluded "developer error, fixed". What is the better analysis?
options: Look across the defects for a common cause, e.g. no time-zone test data or guidelines, and fix that systematically
Accept the three conclusions
Ban time zones from the product
Assign all time-zone work to one developer
questions.explanation: Recurring categories indicate a systemic cause that individual RCAs missed. Fixing test data, guidance and reviews prevents the class of defects. The other options do not address the cause.

questions.prompt: A team runs a fishbone session for frequent failed deployments and lists 25 possible causes. What is the best next step?
options: Use data (e.g. deployment logs) to check which causes actually contributed, then act on the top few
Fix all 25 at once
Pick the cause that the most senior person suggests
Stop because there are too many causes
questions.explanation: A fishbone generates hypotheses; evidence decides which are real. Prioritising the main contributors gives the most improvement for the effort. Fixing everything is unrealistic and seniority is not evidence.
